<!-- page 697 -->
Mr. Osgood began with explaining that they were bringing this to the commission after receiving 
community feedback regarding subdivision regulations. 
There were people from the public there to also give some testimony about the topic. 
He gave a brief summery of why subdivisions were different from just raw land splits but noted that 
unfortunately the public often became confused by the two. 
The issues first arose when the Minor Land Division Ordinance was approved, as property owners felt 
that their rights were infringed upon, as well as intentions of older subdivisions coming into conflict with 
the Ordinance. 
He wanted to have an open discussion about the various issues that had come up from the community 
and the Board of Supervisors informally to help better serve the community with the commission, as 
well as get their feedback for moving forward with a more formal request. He also mentioned that there 
was a committee that was reviewing this and coming up with solutions for this tricky situation. 
The challenges are: 
• The current Subdivision Ordinance requires a denial of splits within subdivisions. 
• Property owners that had previously planned to split their property for years prior to MLD 
Ordinance going into place and are now unable to move ahead with their plans. 
• Some approved Subdivision’s CC&R’s had envisioned and anticipated lot splits, which is in direct 
conflict with the Subdivision Ordinance. 
• This leads to issues getting building permits as the splits that have been done bring a title 
restriction for these lots that are now out of compliance, as well as out of compliance lots 
unable to be issued permits due to being split prior to the MLD Ordinance. 
• There are issues with an unsustainable amount of lots in some subdivision infrastructures 
• There are legal and state statute concerns, once a subdivision is platted and approved by a 
board, you cannot add more lots easily.  Precedents have already been set with the law, and no 
other counties in Arizona have processes outside of the Final Plat Amendment to add lots, or a 
Minor Plat Amendment to adjust lot lines into a subdivision. 
• Various entities including members of the Board of Supervisors, the County Attorney, and the 
County Manager wish to implement a new process or improve the the current processes to 
better serve the public interest. 
• Subdivision regulations are in place for a reason, to ensure proper function of roads, drainage 
and water shed, public utilities such as sanitary, etc. that would be disrupted by the higher 
density that splitting would bring. 
• The Subdivision Ordinance was implemented in 1969, and has not been updated in 15 years.  
Mr. Osgood stated that he wished to implement some sort of hybrid system to help assist people 
that had unique cases. 
Mr. Osgood also provided an example of a subdivision in Heber, Buckskin Artist Community with 
flexible wording that was approved in 1971 with CC&R’s that allows for split once or twice, as 
needed.

<!-- page 698 -->
Commissioner Wendell DeCross asked what the original size of the lots were, Vice Chair Ruth Ann 
Smith was familiar with and had done heavy research into this subdivision’s history stated that they 
were mostly 3 acres in size, and others were 2 acres. She further noted that they were intended not 
to be split down to less than one acre parcels. 
Mr. Osgood stated that the CC&R’s did not have any sort of precedence over the County Ordinance 
or regulations.  He further stated that the original plat was approved for 157 lots, but if they were 
allowed to split as the CC&R’s allowed it would be upwards of 300 lots, which was not sustainable 
through the level of planning that was done for this subdivision. 
The main point was that while the splitting has taken place over the years, it cannot continue the 
way it has. 
Mr. Osgood stated that they had spoken with a variety of stake holders and realtors in the area that 
were intimately familiar with the area, as well as some property owners that were trying to navigate 
the process to achieve their goals, former Commissioner Chuck Teetsel, the County Attorney’s 
Office, professional Engineers, and more. 
His challenge and request for feedback was how they could do some sort of plat alteration process 
that was feasible, or an allowance and listed a few options for criteria for allowing future splits: 
• The Subdivision must have been platted before or around 1969 
• The CC&R’s state that they are allowed to split the property 
o He noted that just because the CC&R’s state that you could split it, does not mean 
that the splits should be allowed in any way, but at least the expectations of the 
property owners could be met. 
• Minimum Lot Size of 1 acre 
• Minimum of 100’ frontage on a publicly dedicated road. 
• Those not aware of the regulations be given a 2 – 3 year moratorium to split their property 
before no further splits would be allowed without a complete replating process. 
• Making the applicants provide proof that the land is buildable, that it pass requirements for 
fire safety and has legal access. 
Chairman Howe thanked John and asked how many subdivisions they’d be looking at within the 
County’s jurisdiction.  John stated that they did not currently have the numbers for the pre-1969. 
Chairman Howe said that the sheer amount of the work needed to be considered, and asked who would 
be responsible for covering the costs. 
John stated that it’s a viable question and stated that if there’s an HOA that has been collecting monies 
for improvements all along it would not be unreasonable for them to be covering the costs and work 
with guidance from the county, but that if the subdivision did not have an active HOA with one property 
owner that was attempting to split it may not be feasible.  Ultimately it came down to needing that final 
plat alteration process to go through, one way or another. 
Vice Chair Smith asked about other areas outside of Heber-Overgaard that had a need for this, John 
stated that there was a property owner in Linden present but was not currently aware of any other

<!-- page 699 -->
areas that needed this kind of attention. Mr. Osgood also noted that perhaps the focus be on the pre-
1969 subdivisions for such consideration. 
Chairman Howe said that putting a moratorium might cause some sort of “Gold Rush” and potentially 
overwhelm staff, or otherwise cause unintended consequences. 
Mr. Osgood said that they had not even considered a process for this yet, and they might also just 
consider that they do it as resources become available, and further noted that there was not any sort of 
requirement that they do any of this. 
Commissioner DeCross asked about the example provided, what the original zoning was, Vice Chair 
stated that it was originally R1-43. 
Commissioner DeCross asked again what the original sizes were, and was unsure what the current sizes 
were on the parcels that had been split several times, Vice Chair Smith explained in further detail. 
Commissioner DeCross noted that County takes precedence over a Home Owners Association, despite 
the HOA’s view that it be otherwise. He stated that just because it was recorded does not make it law, 
nor does it excuse property buyers from their due diligence, and ignorance of the law was no excuse. 
Chairman Howe asked if there was any requirement that the CC&R’s be recorded or approved, Mr. 
Osgood said that they did require them to be recorded, but believed that the Board of Supervisors does  
not approve the CC&R’s. Commissioner DeCross noted that you could record anything. 
Vice Chair Smith disagreed and argued that the intent was important as the Developer had originally 
envisioned these larger lots to be split down. The fact that the CC&R’s were recorded before the 
Ordinance went into place is what caused the contention because the property owners felt that they 
were informed, and that the county has removed their property rights.  
Commissioner Rogers also questioned the unsustainable portion of Mr. Osgood’s description, as he felt 
that was relative as down in the Valley they had homes practically on top of each other that were 
perfectly sustained. He asked if the fact that they were on septic tanks was what the issue of them being 
unsustainable, or if the water lines or power lines were the issue- he felt that it was unfair to just put 
down a “no more splitting” policy as he felt an acre was still fairly large. 
Mr. Osgood spoke to Commissioner Rogers point, noting that they subdivisions in the valley were 
planned to be that way, and that they had infrastructure in place such as sewer, water capacity, and 
carefully planned roadways to accommodate that density in the first place, whereas these had been 
planned and approved to have X amount of density, and now had five times X levels of density. While 
it’s not impossible, it should be replated to capture the requirements that that density would need. 
Chairman Howe agreed that in more populated areas that level of density was required to have planned 
infrastructure, whereas these much older subdivisions if they all went down to 10k square foot lots and 
were all on Septic that that would be unsustainable through state requirements. 
Vice Chair Smith argued that the newer subdivisions had that learning curve, but that it wasn’t fair to 
expect the same level from older subdivisions such as the ones in question. 
The Chairman opened the floor to public comment, for ideas and other such solutions. 
Ryan Elsworth spoke to the commission about his situation.

<!-- page 700 -->
Robert and Chris Packard also spoke to the commission about his experiences, as well. 
Vice Chair Smith further noted that she sympathized with the property owners and felt that this was a 
very case-by-case situation and no matter what there would always be someone impacted negatively, 
and hoped that they would be able to find a better solution for this. 
Commissioner Rogers asked what it was that made the properties out of compliance. 
Mr. Osgood said that the compliance issues had nothing to do with the 2018 MLD Ordinance, and it was 
the actual Subdivision Ordinance, and cited the article 9 and section 9.2 in question.  
Commissioner Rogers asked why the splits had ever been allowed, it was brought up that the zoning 
ordinance allowed the splits, but that the Subdivision Ordinance did not, and that there were conflicting 
regulations. 
Chairman Howe stated that this was a difficult situation as they didn’t want to violate state statute, but 
they wished to find an amicable resolution.   
There was further discussion with the audience and Vice Chair Smith about the need for realtor 
involvement with being notified of the regulations. 
Commissioner Rogers further noted that there might be liability issues with handling these case-by-case, 
especially with conflicting regulations. 
Mr. Osgood said that he couldn’t speak to the legal issues at this time, but that they wanted to put 
something out to the lawmakers and this was quite informative, and that they would work toward 
making a process for this, but that they had an obligation to protect the public at large and have a solid 
legal standing.   
Chairman Howe asked Mr. Osgood if staff could draft a checklist of conditions within the next month 
that need to be evaluated through engineering and building to see if the split could even be accepted in 
the first place, such as a minimum frontage or feet to help further filter for standardizing and ensuring 
safety. 
Commissioner DeCross brought up a legality issue with case-by-case, comparing the issues with Spot 
Zoning. 
Mr. Osgood agreed to move forward with the checklist, but that the next big steps would be the process 
by which the Board of Supervisors makes a policy, no matter what direction it be, either by amending 
the subdivision Ordinance or implementing a process or making it a case-by-case situation. 
Chairman Howe concurred, but was sensitive to the needs for public imput for the case-by-case 
scenarios. 
Vice Chair Smith asked for John to clarify that this would return to the public hearing format, and that 
the team he mentioned would be involved, or what the plan was, Mr. Osgood said that he felt it 
wouldn’t be unusual to bring it back before the Commission and said that it would be wise to have a 
more formal hearing for this.  Vice Chair Smith stated that the ad-hoc committee should participate and 
be involved and provide input to the commission.

Submitted For: Mischa Larisch, Deputy Director of Planning & Development

Motion before the Commission:
PUBLIC HEARING: Consideration of the adoption of Resolution Number 06-2023
approving/denying a Zone Change request by Michael James Barclay for the southern portion
of a 10-acre parcel from R1-10 (Single-Family Residential Zoning) to C-R
(Commercial-Residential) to be consistent with the northern portion which is C-R for the first
300 from northern boundary, White Mountain Lake Road.
Background:
The site is located on APN# 304-22-005, T11N, R22E, S17. Owner: FSBC Properties, LLC.
Agent: Michael James Barclay.
The applicant, Michael Barclay, is requesting a Zone Change to the southern portion of his
property that is currently zoned R1-10 (Single-Family Residential Zoning) to C-R
(Commercial-Residential) to match the northern portion.
The property is situated at the southeast corner of White Mountain Lake Road and Woodside
Trail and used to be Claire’s Corner Swap Meet. Currently, the first 300’ of the property from
WM Lake Road is C-R, and the remaining portion is left R1-10 (Single-Family Residential
Zoning). The new owners, Michael James and Courtney Erin Barclay, plan to build and operate
an RV Park at this location and want to utilize the entire property for their RV Park. Therefore,
this zone change application was initiated.
The applicant(s) will submit a SUP application for the RV Park in the future.
The applicant held a neighborhood meeting by contacting neighbors.
Staff received two calls on the proposal with concerns and against the rezone.
At the January 19, 2023, Planning and Zoning Commission meeting, the neighbor directly
behind the subject property spoke and expressed concerns about C-R 's definition being very
broad and felt the proposal did not serve the community., did not want vacationers in her front
yard, and she was opposed. 
Commissioner Smith asked legal counsel if this would be spot zoning. Since the property is

<!-- page 706 -->
adjacent to the commercial zoning, this would not be considered Spot Zoning Staff answered,
but Mr. Clark offered to meet with Commissioner Smith later on the question with Mischa
Larisch.  Another neighbor, Lawrance Meisner asked the Commission what would happen to
the roadways that are already in poor shape. Staff indicated that these issues will be addressed
when the applicant applies for a SUP application for the RV Park operation. 
The Chairman, Jack Latham indicated he wanted to add a condition that substantial construction
would start within 6 months from the BOS meeting on the site, otherwise the rezoning will
revert to the original. 
Recommendation: 
The Planning Staff and the Planning and Zoning Commission recommend approval of the Zone
Change to the Navajo County Board of Supervisors with the condition of a building permit
being issued, otherwise the rezoning will revert to the original.

BACKGROUND and ANALYSIS:  
 
The applicant, Michael Barclay, is requesting a Zone Change to the southern portion of his property 
that is currently zoned R1-10 (Single-Family Residential Zoning) to C-R (Commercial-Residential) 
to match the northern portion.  
 
The property is situated at the southeast corner of White Mountain Lake Road and Woodside Trail 
and used to be Claire’s Corner Swap Meet.  Currently, the first 300’ of the property from WM Lake 
Road is C-R, and the remaining portion is left R1-10 (Single-Family Residential Zoning).  The new 
owners Michael James and Courtney Erin Barclay plan  to build and operate an RV Park at this 
location and want to utilize the entire property for their RV Park.  Therefore, this zone change 
application was initiated.  
 
The applicant(s) will submit a SUP application for the RV Park in the future.  
 
The applicant held a neighborhood meeting by contacting neighbors.   
 
Staff received two calls on the proposal with concerns and against to the rezone.

Section 1101 - Purpose. 
 
The principal purpose of this zoning district is to conserve and protect single-family residential 
development where minimum lots of not less than ten -thousand (10,000) square feet in area 
are suitable and appropriate taking into consideration existing conditions, including present 
use of land, present lot sizes, future land use needs, and the availability of public utilities.  
Principal uses permitt ed in this zoning district include single -family dwellings, churches, 
schools, parks, playgrounds, and other community facilities. 
 
 
ARTICLE 15 – (C-R) – COMMERCIAL-RESIDENTIAL ZONING DISTRICT 
     
Section 1501 - Purpose. 
The principal purpose of this zoning district is to provide for shops and services in convenient 
locations to meet the daily needs of families in the immediate residential neighborhoods and 
wholesaling or distribution activities in locations where there is  adequate access to major stre ets 
or highways. Principal uses permitted in this zoning district include retail and wholesale 
commerce, commercial entertainment, and some uses of a light manufacturing nature.

4.0 Land Use Element 
4.7 Goals and Policies 
 
Goal 2: To administer the Land Use Element of the Navajo County Comprehensive Plan so as to 
further the purposes of the Plan. 
 
Policy 2-A: Approve zone changes that are consistent with the Land Use Element’s character areas, 
as shown on the Land Use Map. However, the Land Use Element and Map shall not be  used as the 
sole justification for making decisions on zone changes. 
 
 
Goal 7: Facilitate commercial and industrial development, including business and technology 
uses, where appropriate to increase the sales tax and employment opportunities. 
 
Policy 7-A: Encourage strategic placement of commercial development so as to attract and locate 
shopping and employment uses that have paved or other appropriately surfaced access and are  
easily accessible, particularly in or near established communities and cities, and in communities 
with air and/or rail access.

Motion before the Commission:
PUBLIC HEARING: Consideration of the adoption of Resolution Number 07-2023 
approving/denying a Zone Change of a 0.87-acre parcel from A-General (General Zoning
District) to C-R (Commercial-Residential) to build an accounting and tax office. 
Background:
The site is located on APN# 212-09-108Q, T09N, R22E, S09. Owner: White Mountain
Investments, LLC. Agent: Brian A. Brimhall.
The applicant, Brian A. Brimhall, is requesting a Zone Change to his property currently zoned
as A-General (General Zoning District) to C-R (Commercial-Residential Zoning District)
zoning, located on State Route 260 in Lakeside and currently vacant. The purpose of the rezone
is to be able to build an accounting and tax office.
The staff received one call against the proposal and one inquiring for information about the
project with concerns. 
At the January 19, 2023 P&Z Commission meeting, neighbors attended, asked questions and
expressed their concerns.  Mr. Charles Desalme had questions about drainage and Juanita Drive
being a privately maintained driveway and who in the future would be responsible. He stated
that he was opposed to the project. Ms. Julie Quesada also spoke to the Commission with the
same reasons as Mr. Desalme and opposed to rezoning. 
The applicant, Mr. Brimhall  said he is willing to pave and maintain the portion of Juaita Drive
for their driveway. He also noted that ADOT is not willing to install a turn on the site. 
The Planning and Zoning Commission passed a recommendation to approve motion 7-0. 
Recommendation: 
The Planning and Development Services Staff and the Planning and Zoning Commission
recommend approval of the Zone Change to the Navajo County Board of Supervisors.

County boundary, but anything south of Juanita is in the Town of Pinetop- Lakeside jurisdiction.      
Because of the proximity, staff informed the Town of PL of the proposed project, and they did not 
have any issues.  
 
There is residential housing(s) on the rear (east side) of the property and both sides of Juanita Lane.

Meadows) and immediately south, which is in Town of Pinetop- Lakeside jurisdiction and called 
Mountain Gate Subdivision.  The  remaining properties are either vacant or mostly in commercial 
uses along the SR 260.  The Original Zoning Map depicts that several properties along the SR 260 
were originally zoned commercial, but this property was left as A-General.  
The proposed conceptual site plan shows the building location and the parking being placed on the

Section 301 - Purpose.

Ordinance. No subdividing shall be conducted or approved in the "A-General Zone", without prior

specifically listed in this Article. Other uses may be permitted as Special Uses under Article 20. 
 
 
ARTICLE 15 – (C-R) – COMMERCIAL-RESIDENTIAL ZONING DISTRICT

locations to meet the daily needs of families in the immediate residential neighborhoods and 
wholesaling or distribution activities in locations where there is  adequate access to major streets

BACKGROUND and ANALYSIS: 
The applicant, Sunrise Health and Recovery (SHR) is requesting approval of a Special Use Permit 
to operate a licensed Behavioral Health Residential Facility (BHRF) at 965 Full House Lane in the 
Linden area.  
 
The site is located on Full House Lane from SR 260 and there is an existing building, which used to 
function as a nursing home  in the past.  There is a school facility at the southeast corner of the SR 
260 and Full House.  The subject property is located kitty corner from the school.  The school 
property and the residential use on the north side are zoned C-R, Commercial-Residential, the rear, 
the south and cross the street properties are residential uses with A-General zoning.

  North  C-R Residential Use

Navajo County - For Official Use Only 
 
SHR is currently licensed by the State of Arizona - Arizona Department of Health Services  and is 
administered by Dr. Nathan A. Velez to serve Navajo County residents in the White Mountains. The 
license is to operate a 10-bed facility at this location. The operational protocol is stated as follows:  
 
• Audible alarms on all doors and windows that sound when opened. 
• Hourly (or less, as required) rounds to ensure all patients/residents are on site. 
• Prohibit the admission of individuals with a history of sex crimes 
• Prohibit the admission of individuals on the sexual abuse registry 
• Prohibit the use of alcohol or drugs on site 
• Discharge of residents who test positive for alcohol or drugs while in treatment 
• Extensive staff training in safety measures to include verbal de-escalation of altercations 
• Staff member/s are in-house, and awake, 24 hours a day / 7 days a week. 
• Comprehensive therapy for all residents, to include individual, group and family, as well as 12-
step, daily living and Wellbriety sessions. 
• Facility is monitored inside and out with security cameras 24 hours a day / 7 days a week 
• Outside recreational area is fenced to allow freedom of movement within a prescribed area only 
• Random / weekly urine tests on residents for illicit substances. 
 
 
Following information is provided in the narrative by the applicant:  
 
Number of Residents: 
The number of residents at Sunrise Health and Recovery residential facility will  be 10, as licensed 
by Arizona Department of Health Services (ADHS.) 
 
 Length of Stay: 
• The residential program length of stay is determined according to medical need criteria per 
The American Society of Addiction Medicine criteria. All applicants requesting residential 
treatment will be required to complete a Pre-Screen, Inquiry and if eligible an intake followed 
with a comprehensive Clinical Assessment by an Arizona Licensed Behavioral Health 
Professional and Psychiatric evaluation by a Medical Provider prior to admission. 
 
• The length of stay may be on average 1 -30, 60, and/or 90 days; as reviewed and  approved by 
SHR Medical Director and Medicaid/AHCCCS, Insurance, or self-pay. 
 
Staffing: 
• Staff on site weekly; 8: Medical Provider, Clinical Program Director, Administrative Assistant, 
and five (5) Behavioral Health Technicians (BHT’s); once over 8 – 10 residents, SHR will have 
an additional 5 BHT’s for a weekly 
 staffing total of 13 staff per week. 
• ADHS regulations require one staff on shift for 8 residential beds filled and above 8, clinics will 
require two staff on the floor for all shifts. 
• The Monday to Friday Day shift will have three (3) staff assigned, as all  intakes/assessments 
and admissions will occur Monday thru Friday, 8:00 am  until 5:00 pm. Please *Note: Office 
hours will be 8:00am until 5:00pm Monday –Friday. 
• We have three (3) overlapping shifts Monday thru Friday (day, 2nd, and 3rd shifts);two (2) 
overlapping shifts on Saturdays and Sundays (day and night shifts).

• The facility has two locked front entrance doors. The first door has a doorbell.   Once pressed,

window to address the individual(s) requests. 
• All exits/entrances have alarms and are locked 24 hours daily. 
 
Parking:

18. Institutional Residential and other Group Homes. 
 
 
Article 25- General Provisions, Section 2518: 
Section 2518 – Group Homes for the Disabled 
1. Purpose:   The purpose of these regulations is to permit disabled persons, as defined by state

and Arizona state law, while maintaining the residential character of neighborhoods.

Home for the Developmentally Disabled or an Assisted Living Home as defined by state 
statutes, then any such State law or rule shall apply in addition to the conditions listed 
herein and shall preempt any conflicting condition listed herein. 
 
3. Performance Standards:  Group Homes for the Disabled shall be located, developed, and 
operated in compliance with the following standards:

<!-- page 777 -->
Planning and Zoning Commission                                     January 19, 2023        8 | P a g e  
Navajo County - For Official Use Only 
a. Separation: The minimum separation between group homes shall be 1,200 feet as 
prescribed by A.R.S. § 36-582, as measured by the closest property lines. 
b. Occupancy: The number of residents, excluding staff, shall not exceed 10. 
c. Exterior Appearance: There shall be no sign or other exterior indication of a group 
home visible from a street. 
d. Compliance with Building, Environmental Health, and Fire Safety Regulations: Group 
homes shall be required to comply with all relevant building, environmental health, 
and fire safety regulations.  If a group home has one or more non-ambulatory residents, 
building code requirements in addition to those applicable to group homes containing 
no non-ambulatory residents, shall apply. 
e. Licensing: Group homes shall comply with applicable licensing requirements. 
f. Parking: Any parking for the group homes shall be on site. 
 
4. Permits and Administration. 
a. Property is considered a Group Home for the Disabled under this Ordinance after the 
Navajo County Planning and Zoning Department issues a Permit for a Group Home 
for the Disabled for that property.  Only properties serving occupants who fit the 
definition of disabled under the Fair Housing Act are eligible for determination as a 
Group Home for the Disabled. 
b. In order to secure a permit for a group home for the disabled, an application must be 
submitted on t he form prescribed by the Planning and Zoning Department.  The 
application must include the following: 
i. A site plan 
ii. A notarized statement detailing qualifications 
iii. Copies of applicable licenses  
iv. Affidavit of compliance and other documentation indicating the property 
as a group home for the disabled 
v. Any additional information or plans, if deemed necessary 
 
c. If standards are not met, the home shall be considered another group home or 
institutional residential use and shall be subject to the provisions of the Zon ing 
Ordinance guiding such establishments.  Status as a Group Home for the Disabled is 
open to review by the Navajo County Planning and Zoning Department and may be 
cancelled at any time upon a determination by the Director that the property is no 
longer b eing used for a qualifying purpose or meeting standards laid forth in this 
Ordinance.

A “Project Narrative” (2 copies), expressing your reasons for the proposed Special 
Use Permit and how it will be beneficial to the area, and including an explanation of 
the proposed use, a schedule for its development, and the compatibility of the

Sunrise Health and Recovery (SHR) seeks to operate under a Special Use Permit a Licensed 
Behavioral Health Residential Facility (BHRF). SHR is currently licensed by the State of 
Arizona-Arizona Department of Health Services and meets all registered criteria for such use.  
SHR seeks to operate in the Show Low, Arizona area as there is a high demand and 
concentrate of Substance Use/Misuse, Opiate Use Dependence and published material in the 
local Navajo County Press about a need for treatment facilities to assist in this epidemic. 
According the 2020 Navajo County Overdose Fatality Review (Attached) key factors identified 
included improved “access to care” in the immediate area, an increase of Medication Assisted 
Treatment (MAT) in the area, “improved coordination of care” between hospitals, jails and 
treatment facilities. Additionally, it is noted that “South County” of Navajo (Snowflake, Taylor, 
Show Low) are were most prevalent cases of Opiate Overdose fatalities occur. As such, 
Fentanyl accounted for 48% and Alcohol 32% of all overdoses in Navajo County, both carry 
potential lethal overdose potential. SHR and its leadership believes this is a very beneficial 
opportunity to both the local Navajo County area and greater Navajo County Region. Providing 
a service to save lives and enhance recovery places residents back into our community as 
contributors to our local communities and reduces crime, increases employment and keeps 
families united.  
 
SHR is administered by a long-time local Navajo County Resident, Dr. Nathan A. Velez, Phd, 
LPC, LPC who served in a decade long capacity both as a treatment provider and Deputy 
Probation Officer to Navajo County. Dr. Velez identifies this use of a BHRF in the Show Low 
area can be of service to not only all of Navajo County Residents, but specifically target the area 
affected the most. It is Dr. Velez’s passion to serve the residents of Navajo County, in this 
particular area as he describes “far too often our people of Navajo County are having to leave 
the area or state to get much needed treatment, often leaving their community and families, who 
are essential to the healing and change process.” As a part of recovery and treatment, “it is 
essential to heal within the community.” In addition, the SHR Center is Directed Clinically by a 
local Substance Abuse Recovery Expert, and longtime Navajo County resident and recovery 
advocate, Eugene “Ed” Gonzales. Ed has served the Navajo County community for over 30 
years in the helping profession and eagerly awaits to help service in the capacity of Clinical 
Director of SHR to ensure our people of Navajo County obtain the best evidenced based care. 
Mr. Gonzales, also was instrumental in starting Navajo County Drug Court over 1 decade ago 
with now presiding Judge Dale Nielsen and C.A. Brad Carylon. His passion for helping those in 
recovery is a blessing to the communities of Navajo County. In short, between Dr. Velez and Mr. 
Gonzales, a combined 60 years of experience servicing the communities of Navajo County 
Exist.  
The schedule for development is a Grand Opening to the public to be of transparency and to 
allow the community to visit and see the elements of the treatment center. It is of tremendous 
importance for SHR to be a part of the community, while operating within the community. The

<!-- page 786 -->
parcel of land and privacy of the location of the facility also serves tremendous purpose for 
those who are healing and in recovery. The connection to nature, privacy from the city and 
ability to focus on their care are essential to the residents of Navajo County in recovery. The 
location provides the ability to and opportunity to heal in nature. Thus, our slogan, “Recovery in 
the Pines.” Attached you will find our website for additional information and questions: 
www.sunrisehealthandrecovery.com. You will also find a list of stakeholders who are supportive 
of the BHRF to include the local criminal justice sector leaders (Navajo County Probation and 
County Attorney) Jason Cash and Brad Carlyon, Blue Cross Blue Shield CEO and President 
Shawn NAU (Northern Az Medicaid Plan) and many others.  
 
SHR appreciates the concerns that may be expressed by the community in regards to the 
location of our facility and the type of residents SHR proposes to serve.  SHR has taken multiple 
steps to ensure the safety of the community, staff and residents.  To that end, SHR has 
implemented the following protocols and safety measures: 
 Audible alarms on all doors and windows that sound when opened. 
 Hourly (or less, as required) rounds to ensure all patients/residents are on site. 
 Prohibit the admission of individuals with a history of sex crimes 
 Prohibit the admission of individuals on the sexual abuse registry 
 Prohibit the use of alcohol or drugs on site 
 Discharge of residents who test positive for alcohol or drugs while in treatment 
 Extensive staff training in safety measures to include verbal de-escalation of altercations 
 Staff member/s are in-house, and awake, 24 hours a day / 7 days a week.  
 Comprehensive therapy for all residents, to include individual, group and family, as well 
as 12-step, daily living and Wellbriety sessions. 
 Facility is monitored inside and out with security cameras 24 hours a day / 7 days a 
week 
 Outside recreational area is fenced to allow freedom of movement within a prescribed 
area only 
 Random / weekly urine tests on residents for illicit substances 
 
SHR believes that by taking the above measures, it can best mitigate the concerns of the 
surrounding community and ensure the safety of all involved.  
 
To address other concerns voiced regarding number or residents, duration of stay, etc.: 
 Number of Residents:  
o The number of residents at Sunrise Health and Recovery residential facility will 
be 10, as licensed by Arizona Department of Health Services (ADHS.) 
 Length of Stay: 
o The residential program length of stay is determined according to medical need 
criteria per The American Society of Addiction Medicine criteria. All applicants 
requesting residential treatment will be required to complete a Pre-Screen, 
Inquiry and if eligible an intake followed with a comprehensive Clinical

<!-- page 787 -->
Assessment by an Arizona Licensed Behavioral Health Professional and 
Psychiatric evaluation by a Medical Provider prior to admission.  
o The length of stay may be on average 1-30, 60, and/or 90 days; as reviewed and 
approved by SHR Medical Director and Medicaid/AHCCCS, Insurance, or self-
pay. 
 
 Staffing: 
o Staff on site weekly; 8: Medical Provider, Clinical Program Director, 
Administrative Assistant, and five (5) Behavioral Health Technicians (BHT’s); 
once over 8 – 10 residents, SHR will have an additional 5 BHT’s for a weekly 
staffing total of 13 staff per week. 
o ADHS regulations require one staff on shift for 8 residential beds filled and above 
8, clinics will require two staff on the floor for all shifts.  
o The Monday to Friday Day shift will have three (3) staff assigned, as all 
intakes/assessments and admissions will occur Monday thru Friday, 8:00 am 
until 5:00 pm.  Please *Note: Office hours will be 8:00am until 5:00pm Monday – 
Friday.  
o We have three (3) overlapping shifts Monday thru Friday (day, 2nd, and 3rd shifts); 
two (2) overlapping shifts on Saturdays and Sundays (day and night shifts). 
o The facility has two locked front entrance doors. The first door has a doorbell. 
Once pressed, staff will open the front door to address the individual(s), as 
indicated they may be invited to the building waiting area where there is a 2nd 
door that is locked to public access with a sliding window to address the 
individual(s) requests.  
o All exits/entrances have alarms and are locked 24 hours daily.  
 
 Parking:  
o We have 2 identified / marked handicapped parking and 12 regular parking 
spaces.   
o Residents do NOT have vehicles parked at the facility.  
  
 Residents Use of Facility: 
o Residents will be allowed the use of the fenced in back yard during the day and 
early evening, while being supervised, during specified free periods only.   
o At all other times, the residents will be in the building for intensive therapy 
sessions related to maintaining their sobriety, meals, and other group / individual 
sessions and activities. Reminder: all doors and windows are alarmed, so staff 
will know if either are opened and can investigate. 
o Residents do not “come and go” daily.  This is an in-patient, residential facility 
providing therapy and counseling to individuals who are at risk of “backsliding” 
and losing their sobriety. SHR provides therapy and the tools needed to stay 
sober and become productive members of society. 
o Family therapy sessions may be held during normal work day hours, 8 am to 5 
pm, by appointment. 
o Resident’s will be allowed 30-minute personal visits with family on weekends and 
by appointment only.

<!-- page 788 -->
 Expected trips to the site, any commercial deliveries, etc.: 
o Minimal traffic to site, residential treatment center will be by appointment, locked 
facility not a public facility for traffic. 
o Only scheduled individuals will be invited and allowed onto SHR property.  
o All entering will be required to sign-in and agree to confidentiality/HIPPA rules. All 
pre-scheduled appointments will indicate reason for visit and will be provided a 
“Visitor” badge; and escorted to identified area allowed; such as a family visit 
(only on Saturday and/or Sunday,) or Administrators Office. 
o There may be a weekly day trip to a local wellness facility such as a gym or pool, 
to provide exercise for our residents 
o SHR plans to offer a once-a-week scheduled visit by a yoga instructor who will 
come to the facility and lead an on-site yoga class for our residents.   
o Our contracted Primary Care Provider or his staff will come a minimum of two 
times per week to ensure the physical wellbeing of our residents. 
o Regarding “commercial deliveries,” SHR anticipates the following: 
 Weekly trash pickup 
 Weekly or bi-weekly grocery delivery 
 Monthly propane check / delivery 
 Monthly, semi-monthly, or as needed deliveries for office supplies from 
such places as Amazon.

General Description: Sunrise Health and Recovery, LLC (SHR) is licensed to operate as a 10 bed Behavioral Health 
Residential Facility (RTC). SHR specializes in treating chemical abuse/dependency, and other addictive and mental health 
disorders. SHR continuum of care begins with a focus on identifying and treating the underlying causal conditions that 
lead to Substance Use and Abuse (SUD’s) addictive behavior; transitioning individuals into sustaining a Wellness 
Recovery Action Plan (WRAP), to achieve a sustainable long term, hopeful for a lifetime in a Recovery Lifestyle.  
 
Sunrise Health and Recovery offers a cost and individualized effective solutions for adult men and women who struggle 
with addiction and chronic relapse.  SHR will provide services for people that will need a continuum of care beyond the 
traditional 30-60 days of residential care. Our belief is that by offering a safe and nurturing therapeutic environment, the 
client will be able to have a variety of controlled experiences which will allow them to find their own path to long term 
wellness in sobriety and growth.  
 
SHR encompasses dignity and respect in an environment designed to be culturally sensitive, provide evidenced based 
program modalities, which incorporate a faceted focus on the individual to build confidence, self worth, esteem and the 
knowledge and wisdom to make better choices for self, family and community. Overall, the SHR Program emphasizes 
wellness in life:  
 MATRIX, a Cognitive Behavioral Therapy, a modality of substance use disorder treatment, as a psychological 
treatment demonstrated to be effective in a range of problems including depression, anxiety disorders, alcohol 
and drug use problems, marital problems, eating disorders and severe mental illness, 
 
 WELLBRIETY, achieving sobriety and abstinence from substance abuse and misuse without stopping there. It 
means going beyond “clean and sober” by entering a journey of healing and balance - mentally, physically, 
emotionally and spiritually. 
 
 SAMSHA: Eight Dimensions of Wellness: SAMHSA's Wellness Initiative supports embracing the Eight 
Dimensions of Wellness: emotional, environmental, financial, intellectual, occupational, physical, social, and 
spiritual to achieve longevity in learned Recovery Lifestyle changes and improved quality of life. 
 
 VIA Character Strengths Classifications: With these criteria of observed six main virtues that emerged in 
societies across the world and across time. Within each of these virtues are several characters strengths that relate to 
displaying or enacting the virtue: Wisdom and Knowledge: Creativity, Curiosity, Open-mindedness, Love of 
learning, Perspective; Courage: Bravery, Persistence, Integrity, Vitality; Humanity: Love, Kindness, Social 
intelligence; Justice: Citizenship, Fairness, Leadership; Moderation/Temperance: Forgiveness and mercy, 
Humility/Modesty, Prudence, Self-regulation; Transcendence: Appreciation of beauty and excellence, Gratitude, 
Hope/Optimism, Humor, Spirituality and ZEST. 
 
  Medication-assisted treatment (MAT) is used to treat substance use disorders as well as sustain recovery and 
prevent overdose. All entering will be assessed with a Psychiatric Evaluation; Medical Team will monitor. 
 
SHR will introduce 12 step model(s) for a strong emphasis on individual involvement.  Provide a strong focus on social 
responsibility and independent living skills. SHR’s continuum care is monitored by Clinical and Medical Teams.  Our 
EMR is Lightning Step Software, which provides: Best Practices Documentation, Real-time Data Access, Flexible & 
Powerful Reporting, Managed Care, Performance Outcomes, Billing/Daily Scheduling, and Security/Privacy (HIPAA) 
 
SHR staffs are licensed behavioral health professionals or behavior health technicians under the direct supervision of a 
behavior health professional.  Progression is based on the client’s ability to successfully accomplish goals, to meet 
objectives agreed and established in their treatment plan.  Please feel to contact me at any time, appreciated.

Dear Navajo County Board of Supervisors and Planning and Zoning Commissioners, 
As a 30-year resident of Navajo County, I have seen the horrible effects of substance use 
and how it escalated further during the pandemic. I know many individuals who lost 
their lives or a family member due to this disease. 
Based on data from the 2020 CHNA update, alcohol/drug use is the seventh most 
common primary reason for a hospital stay and is involved in more than 2,000 hospital 
stays as the primary or other reason for the visit for Navajo County residents. Alcohol 
deaths in Navajo County continued to rise from 65.9 per 100,000 in 2017 to 71.8 in 
2019. Four times the Arizona average of 17.6 (Navajo County CHNA 2020). 
Too often, drugs and alcohol are used to self-medicate co-occurring mental health issues 
brought on by trauma, mostly childhood (i.e., poverty, neglect, physical and sexual 
abuse). In 2019 there were almost 600 hospital stays by Navajo County residents related 
to suicides, suicide attempts, and intentional self-inflicted injuries (2020 Navajo County 
CHNA update). 
Recently I was notified that the Arizona Department of Health Services had approved a 
License for Sunrise Health and Recovery to operate a ten-bed Behavioral Health 
Residential Treatment Facility (RTC) at 965 Full House Rd in Linden. As I understand 
and support, the program will provide a higher level of treatment for individuals with 
chemical use/dependency and other substance and mental health disorders. 
As I have been made aware, Sunrise Health and Recovery care focuses on therapy, has a 
Medical Team to provide medication-assisted treatment, Licensed Professional 
Therapist, and skilled Support Specialists to provide 24 hours a day services and 
coverage. 
Our residents need RECOVERY; to achieve and maintain recovery, we must focus on 
TREATMENT! I support addressing the need to offer help and support for individuals 
suffering from substance use seeking recovery, the opportunity to develop and achieve 
therapy to sustain a long-term, 100% substance free individualized Recovery Lifestyle. 
With my support, I encourage Sunrise Health and Recovery the ability to be granted the 
“Special Permit.” 
Sincerely, 
Allison Hephner

Department of Health Services has approved a License to operate a 10 bed Behavioral Health 
Residential Treatment Facility (RTC), at 965 Full House Rd in Linden. As I understand and 
support, the program will provide a higher level of treatment for individuals with chemical 
use/dependency, and other substance and mental health disorders.  
 
Sunrise Health and Recovery care focuses on therapy, has a Medical Team to provide for 
medication assisted treatment, Licensed Professional Therapist and skilled Support Specialists to 
provide 24 hours a day services and coverage.  
I have been aware of the Opioid Epidemic and have suffered from opioid addiction myself.  In 
my personal recovery, I have known and lost 5 people from opioid overdose and witnessed their 
attempts to get treatment but did not make it through due to lack of resources and the confidence 
and hope they needed to get help. We all have choices in life however, Navajo County lacks in a 
higher-level treatment facility that provides Medication Assisted Treatment (MAT). Sunrise 
Health and Recovery would provide that for addicts that need to get help and would offer them 
the ability to titrate off chemical dependency. 
I support addressing the need to offer help and support for individuals suffering from substance 
use seeking recovery, the opportunity to develop and achieve therapy to sustain long term, 100% 
a substance free individualized Recovery Lifestyle.  
With my full and compassionate support, I encourage Sunrise Health and Recovery the ability to 
be granted the “Special Permit” in order to offer a safe and nurturing therapeutic environment, 
with client-centered focus on a variety of controlled experiences which will allow individuals to 
find their own path to long term wellness in sobriety and growth. 
 
If you have any, please feel free to contact me.

PETITION 
The undersigned persons respectfully request that the Navajo County Planning and Zoning 
Commission recommend, and if recommended, the Board of Supervisors grant request for 
Special Use Permit 22-010 Sunrise Health and recovery Residential Facility District IV regarding 
APN #409-25-003B for the following reasons: 
1. Sunrise Health and Recovery (SHR) Residential Treatment Center (RTC) is licensed to 
operate a 10-bed residential facility by the Arizona Department of Health Services.  This 
facility will provide 30-, 60-, or 90-day in-house treatment to individuals recovering from 
substance abuse disorders.  
2. Listed below are facts and accurate data regarding the proposed use of the facility: 
a. Addiction is a Disease; alcoholics and/or addicts are sick; SHR offers life-saving therapy 
services. 
b. Our property is secured with all doors locked; internal/external surveillance cameras 
are monitored. 
c. Fully trained personnel provide 24-hour supervision, 7 days a week. 
d. Clinical and Medical Teams will assess, evaluate and develop treatment based on 
Medical Need. 
e. Referrals are by phone, admissions arrive for placement; sober/clean from 
detox/hospital, community. 
f. No gatherings/congregating will be tolerated on property. 
g. Clients will remain indoors at all times, only allowed out the back on the fenced 
patio/property. 
h. Admissions, supplies delivered, and staff parking will only be allowed on the parking 
lot. 
i. Individuals of suspect, wandering the neighborhood, will not be enrolled at our facility; 
decisions to contact local authorities will be made for safety interventions. 
j. SHR offers individuals and their families the opportunity to heal in “Wellness” with 
therapeutic services 
k. Our Goal: develop and sustain the opportunity to live 100% substance free; long term 
Recovery Lifestyle. 
l. SHR held an Open House on Sept. 1,2022, which was highly attended with positive 
feedback from neighbors and community. 
m. Our Clinical Program Director has 30+ years as an Administrator and Clinical Director; 
SHR is his 7th residential/outpatient clinic.  He is an addict in recovery with 34 Years 
34 Years Sober/Clean.  
n. Safety is always the #1 priority. 
o. With Dignity and Respect, approval of the “Special Permit,” is one step towards a 
SOLUTION to treat substance abuse, use, and disorders in the White Mountains.

RESOLUTION ____-23 
 
A RESOLUTION OF THE NAVAJO COUNTY BOARD OF SUPERVISORS APPROVING 
A SPECIAL USE PERMIT FOR SUNRISE HEALTH AND RECOVERY RESIDENTIAL 
FACILITY. 
 
WHEREAS, an application for a Special Use Permit  was duly filed on  November 03, 
2022 by Onkar Bhowra to operate Sunrise Health and Recovery Residential Facility; and 
 
WHEREAS, the application concerns the following real property in Navajo County:  
APN# # 409-25-003B, T10N, R21E, S09; and 
 
WHEREAS, the application was considered by the Navajo County Planning & Zoning 
Commission at a duly noticed public hearing on January 19, 2023; and 
 
WHEREAS, the Navajo County Board of Supervis ors after considering the testimony 
and other evidence presented at the hearing, as well as  the recommendations of staff, found that 
the Special Use Permit is consistent with the public health, safety and general welfare and should 
be approved; and 
 
NOW, THEREFORE BE IT R ESOLVED the Board of Supervisors  hereby 
approve the Special Use Permit, subject to the following conditions: 
 
1. The permitted Special Use shall allow maximum of 10 residents at the facility.  
2. The Fire Department requirements shall be met at all times.  
3. No building or structure shall not be occupied prior to complete compliance with all 
appropriate Building Department requirements. 
4. All lighting on the property shall be shielded to reflect downward, be motion- activated, 
and be in conformance with the Navajo County Lighting Ordinance. 
5. The permitted Special Use shall be allowed to occur per the attached/approved site plan.  
Any expansion or change of the Special Use shall require an amendment to this Permit. 
6. This Special Use Permit shall run with the land pending compliance with all County, 
State, and Federal requirements.   
7. If the permitted Special Use is not utilized within a twelve (1 2) month period, from the 
date of Board approval, this permit shall become null and void.

Board of Supervisors Regular 8. c. 1. a.        
Meeting Date: 02/28/2023  
Title: Professional Services Contract with Tomhave Group, Inc.
Submitted For: Madhav Mundle, Public Works Director 
Submitted By: Jeanine Carruthers, Deputy Director Administration
Department: Public Works
Motion before the Board:
Professional Services Contract with the Tomhave Group, Inc.
Background:
The Tomhave Group, Inc. has been providing professional services to assist with working with
our federal partners to create the plan  and appropriations needed to reconstruct the Winslow
Levee. This contract will continue those efforts and work with Congress to explicitly reauthorize
the Army Corps of Engineers to resume its 1043(b) program so that the County can receive
Winslow Levee’s federal construction funds up front and manage its project delivery in lieu of
the Army Corps of Engineers. Clarification about  the consequences of new congressional
language regarding advance fund agreements is also necessary to ensure there is a clearly
defined  range of options. These are but a few of the federal water project issues that should be
addressed for Navajo County.
Additionally, the Tomhave Group will explore newly authorized federal programs for:
• local communities impacted by coal operation closures;
• local governments/facilities impacted by drought conditions; and
• local leaders interested in microgrids to improve the safety and efficiency of critical
infrastructure.

WHEREAS, District requires certain professi onal services for advocating for the

NOW, THEREFORE, the parties agree as follows: 
 
1. Services.  Consultant shall perform the work described in the Scope of Work dated 
February 9, 2023, and those ad ditional items set forth in the Consultant’s schedule 
and fee proposal dated February 9, 2023, in a competent and professional manner to 
the satisfaction of District.  The Scope of Work and the Consultant’s schedule and fee 
proposal are attached hereto and by this reference incorporat ed herein.  If any 
incorporated term is inconsistent with the Agreement, this Agreement shall control. 
 
2. Consultant’s Expertise.  Consultant warrants that it has the ability, authority, 
capacity and professional expertise to perfo rm this Agreement.  Consultant shall 
provide an adequate staff of experienced  personnel, capable of and devoted to the 
successful accomplishment of the work to be performed hereunder.  Consultant shall 
assign specific individuals to key positio ns.  Once assigned to work under this 
Agreement, key personnel shall not be removed or replaced without District’s prior 
written approval.  
 
3. Independent Contractor.  Consultant acknowledges that  it is an independent 
contractor.  Neither party is or shall purport to be an agent, employee, partner, joint 
venturer or associate of the other.  An employee or agen t of one party shall not be 
deemed an employer or agent  of the other party for any purpose.  Taxes or Social 
Security contributions will not be with held from any paymen t by District, and 
Consultant shall be solely responsible for such matters.

the work to be performed hereunder without District’s prior written approval.  All 
subcontracts shall comply with applicable federal and state laws and regulations and 
shall impose on the subcontractor substantially the same obligations as are imposed 
on Consultant by this Agreement with respect to those matters covered by Sections 8, 
9, 10, 12, 15 and 18.  Consultant is  responsible for full performance of this 
Agreement regardless of whether subcontractors are used. 
 
5. Time for Completion.  Consultant’s services will be provided in a manner consistent 
with the degree of care and skill ordi narily exercised by me mbers of the same 
profession currently practicing under similar circumstances.  Consultant’s services 
shall be performed as expeditiously as is consistent with professional skill and care 
and the orderly progress of the Project, and in accord ance with an agreed upon 
schedule for the performance of the Services hereunder.  Time limits established by a 
schedule approved by District shall not, except for reasonable cause, be exceeded by 
District or Consultant.  The Schedule shall be adjusted, if necessary, as the Project 
proceeds.  The date for final performance shall be extended by the number of days 
that performance is delayed by governmental approval or review procedures or other 
causes beyond Consultant’s reasonable control, as jointly confirmed in writing by the 
parties’ representatives. 
 
6. Payment.  District shall pay to Consultant  a not-to-exceed sum of forty eight 
thousand dollars ($48,000.00) as  payment in full for a ll services rendered by 
Consultant pursuant to this Agreement.  Pa yments shall be made within 30 days of 
District’s receipt of Consul tant’s monthly invoices.  E ach invoice shall detail the 
work performed during the billing period. 
 
7. Defects in Work.  District may reject any work product that fails to meet customary 
professional standards or Project specifi cations.  Consultant agrees to promptly 
remedy all such deficiencies.  The parties shall make a good faith effort to resolve any 
controversy or claim through informal nego tiation as set forth in Section 12.  No 
compensation shall be paid for any reject ed work until such issues have been 
resolved.

12. Negotiation of Disputes.  The parties shall make a good faith effort to resolve any

13. Suspension and Termination by District: 
 
A. Suspension.  District may, without cause, order Consultant in writing to suspend, 
delay or interrupt its performance in whole or part.  An adjustment shall be made 
to the completion date and for any increase in the cost of performance resulting 
from the suspension, delay or interruption.  No adjustment shall be made to the 
extent that performance is or would have been suspended, delayed or interrupted 
by another cause for which Consultant is responsible. 
 
B. Termination for Cause.   District may terminate th is Agreement for cause if 
Consultant refuses or fails to supply enough properly skilled workers to perform 
this Agreement; fails to make required payments to subcontractors; disregards 
laws, ordinances, rules, regulations or  orders of a public  authority having 
jurisdiction; or otherwise commits a material breach of  this Agreement.  When 
any of the foregoing causes exist, District shall give Consultant written notice and 
a ten-day opportunity to cure the default.  If the default remains uncured, District 
may (without prejudice to any other rights or remedies it may have) terminate this 
Agreement and finish the work or cause it to be finished.  If the unpaid balance of 
the Agreement exceeds the cost of fini shing the work (including any expenses 
incurred by District as a re sult of Consultant’s defa ult), Consultant shall be 
entitled to payment for its performance up to the amount of such excess.  If the 
cost of finishing the work exceeds the u npaid balance, Consultant shall pay the 
difference to District. 
 
C. Termination for Convenience.  District, by written notice to Consultant, may 
terminate this Agreement in whole or part when in the sole discretion of District it 
is in District’s best interests to do so.  Consultant sh all be paid for all material, 
equipment and services provided, as well as reasonable termination expenses and 
a reasonable allowance for profit and overhead, provided that such payments, 
exclusive of termination expenses, shal l not exceed the total amount payable 
pursuant to Section 6 less any paymen ts previously made to Consultant.

Date: Feb. 9, 2023
To: Madhav Mundle P.E, Public Works Director
From: Jeff & Brandy Tomhave
Memo: New Contract Proposal
The Tomhave Group is pleased to propose continuation of our work for Navajo County 
to advocate for the federal policy making and assistance that is needed to help you 
protect the public safety and economic opportunities of your residents through public 
works.
Historically, we have worked with you and your federal partners to create the plan and 
appropriations needed to reconstruct the Winslow Levee. We propose continuing our 
role in his historic eﬀort. This year, it is critically important to get Congress to explicitly 
reauthorize the Army Corps of Engineers to resume its 1043(b) program so that you 
can receive Winslow Levee’s federal construction funds up front and manage its 
project delivery in lieu of the Army Corps of Engineers. Clari ﬁcation about the 
consequence of new congressional language regarding advance fund agreements is 
also necessary to ensure that you have a clearly deﬁned range of options. These are 
but a few of the federal water project issues that we know should be addressed for 
Navajo County and we feel uniquely qualiﬁed to advocate your interests in Washington, 
DC.
Additionally, we are eager to explore with you newly authorized federal programs for:
•local communities impacted by coal operation closures;
•local governments/facilities impacted by drought conditions; and
•local leaders interested in microgrids to improve the safety and eﬃciency of critical 
infrastructure.

<!-- page 859 -->
We have already shared with you our detailed outline of opportunities in the FY23 
Omnibus Bill that would likely beneﬁt Navajo County. There are many new federal 
programs funded to make transformational investments in communities just like yours. 
We respectfully propose to continue our partnership with you to work on these speciﬁc 
issues, and any other emergent priorities that require representation for Navajo County 
in Washington DC. The monthly retainer for this contract should remain $4,000 per 
month.  Any travel costs associated with the performance of this contract will be born 
by us.

EXECUTIVE SESSION pursuant to A.R.S. §38-3403.03(A)(3) for the Board to receive legal

WOIA's Local Workforce Development Board voted on or about November 20, 2022, to

Resources Network (NACRN).  This board is being asked to ratify that decision.
